# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–6 (Complete and Final – Updated 73)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer and autumn of first year; winter of first year; Vauxhall evening during spring of first year; spring of second year; summer of second year (current narrative point); narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford, Chiswick Mall, Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, Southampton Row, Vauxhall, Exeter 'Change, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Budgebudge, Calcutta, Dumdum), Forty Thieves theatre, King's 14th regiment post, Highbury Barn, Covent Garden Market, Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, Bedford tavern, Thames Street (City), Royal Gardens, Quenwick, Wilhaven, St. George's Hanover Square, Lambeth Palace, Cheltenham, Great Gaunt Street, Queen's Crawley (Hants), Mudbury, Gaunt Square, Mansion House, Oxford Street, Swallow Street, Cambridge, Leakington, Squashmore, Bethesda Chapel Liverpool, Naples, Paris, Eton, Pumpernickel, Strasburg, Crawley parish, Yarlton, Quashimaboo, Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Roxby, Wapshot Hall, Christchurch, Rectory House, Hampshire, Chiswick, Coldcombe, Humdrum Hall
- **Narrative Presence**: Narrator warns Vanity Fair is "a very vain, wicked, foolish place, full of all sorts of humbugs and falsenesses and pretensions"; notes "I, for my part, have known a five-pound note to interpose and knock up a half century's attachment between two brethren"

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Married with infant son; established pattern of two yearly visits to Grange; Dorothea's life mixed result of young, noble impulse

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- Inhabit Stone Court in white-haired placidity; Fred becomes distinguished county farmer with work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding"; three boys only, youngest resembles grandfather

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background**: Age nineteen; father artist/drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's academy (clever, prone to debt/taverns, beat wife/daughter when drunk, died after third delirium tremens); mother French opera-girl; claims descent from Entrechats family of Gascony (ancestry verified with D'Hozier's dictionary); had dismal precocity of poverty
- **Education**: Pupil of Miss Pinkerton at Chiswick; received out of charity; Miss Pinkerton notes her appearance disagreeable, parents disreputable, but talents considerable; dread that mother's principles (represented as French Countess fleeing revolutionary horrors, actually person of very lowest order and morals) might prove hereditary; but principles hitherto correct
- **Appearance**: Small, slight, pale, sandy-haired with large odd attractive eyes; white slender fingers
- **Accomplishments**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent; skilled musician, linguist, artist; sings better than Amelia; proficient in globes; studied under Signor Clementi on piano
- **Character**: Determined, never blushed since age eight; capable of calculated charm; observant; thinks "I might go farther, and fare worse"; cares nothing for pupils; understands people's schemes immediately; determined to make herself agreeable to advance her position
- **Joseph Sedley Romance Campaign**: Upon learning of his wealth, determined to marry him; won over entire household; Joseph began eloquent speech "O Miss Sharp, how--" but stopped when music ended; at Vauxhall took Jos's arm, lost in solitary walk, fell into his arms at Moscow panorama; during inebriation Jos shouted "Stop, my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; George Osborne pushed Jos back; Jos never came; household (except Amelia) turned against Rebecca; Blenkinsop reported her reading Mrs. Sedley's letters and accessing trinket boxes; Pinner suspected her of taking Amelia's white ribbing; accepted Amelia's generous presents; received purse from Mr. Sedley, kissed his hand asking him to be her kind protector
- **Journey to Queen's Crawley**: Immediately counted guineas and planned future; at Leakington forced outside coach due to heavy rain and Sir Pitt's proprietorship; rode outside in rain; young Cantab sheltered her; carriage arrival in state through mile-long avenue with lodge-gate having serpent and dove pillars (Crawley arms supporters)
- **First Evening**: Sir Pitt in night-cap and dressing-gown seized her candle, threatened nightly visits unless she's in bed by eleven; called her "pretty little hussy"; two bloodhounds let loose at night (Gorer killed man, Aroarer too old to bite)
- **First Dinner**: Served as family except on company days; wore Amelia's muslin gown; pupils Rose and Violet (thin, ages ten and eight); dinner included mouton aux navets, ale and water in wine-glasses for young ladies; after dinner jug of hot water with rum case-bottle placed before Sir Pitt; offered choice between sermons or pamphlet on corn-laws
- **Governess Duties**: Recognizes Lady Crawley (Rosa) indolent, void of character; treats her with cool respect but focuses on rest of family; does not overtax young brains; reads with Rose delightful French and English works—Dr. Smollett, Henry Fielding, Monsieur Crebillon the younger, Monsieur de Voltaire, "Humphrey Clinker," French plays (claiming to Mr. Crawley it's for French idiom); with Violet promises secrecy about peccadilloes if she'll be good; plays backgammon with Sir Pitt
- **With Mr. Pitt Crawley**: Shows respectful obedience; consults him on French passages; accepts his aid; shows interest in his Quashimaboo-Aid Society speech and malt pamphlet; affected to tears by his evening discourses; says "Oh, thank you, sir" with sighs and upward looks to heaven; Mr. Crawley believes "Blood is everything," believes her mother was Montmorency, thinks himself too fine for common people
- **Current Status**: Has "come round" everybody; writes Sir Pitt's letters, does his business, manages his accounts; has upper hand of whole house—Lady Crawley, Mr. Crawley, the girls and all; Mrs. Bute Crawley now taken great fancy to her (PLAN: Mrs. Bute hopes to secure her as piano professor for her children using Rebecca's talents); Rebecca sees through Mrs. Bute's schemes but shall make herself agreeable; wears Amelia's India muslin and pink silk, now well worn; signs herself "Your poor little Rebecca"

**Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Financial History**: Estate never recovered from heavy fine on Walpole Crawley (first baronet) for peculation in Tape and Sealing Wax Office; now cellars not burgundy-filled, kennels not hound-filled, stables not gallant hunter-filled
- **Character and Behavior**: Old, stumpy, short, vulgar, very dirty man in old clothes and shabby gaiters; smoking horrid pipe; shining bald head, leering red face, twinkling grey eyes, mouth perpetually on grin; country accent; swears great deal; incessantly discusses himself; could not spell and did not care to read
- **Financial Practices**: Almost invincible repugnance to paying anybody; could only be brought by force to discharge debts; said "What's the good of being in Parliament if you must pay your debts?"
- **Parliamentary Position**: High sheriff; had higher place in Vanity Fair than most brilliant genius or spotless virtue
- **Family Relations**: First marriage to Griselda/Grizzel (sixth daughter of Mungo Binkie, Lord Binkie); owes son Mr. Pitt Crawley sum from jointure of his mother
- **Current Status**: Miss Crawley has arrived with fat horses, fat servants, fat spaniel; has seventy thousand pounds in five per cents; Rawdon and Sir Pitt struggle to settle her cushions and hand her coffee; she complains about her toady Miss Briggs at home, calls her brothers her toadies

**Mr. Pitt Crawley (Eldest Son)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Character and Manner**: Pale, thin, ugly, silent; thin legs, no chest; hay-coloured whiskers and straw-coloured hair; in full dress pompous as undertaker; very picture of sainted mother Griselda; very earnest; high-bred propriety; seldom spoke to Rosa, but with powerful respect
- **School Experience**: At Eton called "Miss Crawley"; younger brother Rawdon licked him violently; never punished during eight years despite mediocre parts made up by meritorious industry
- **Career**: Studied ancient and modern orators with assiduity; speaking unceasingly at debating societies; had fine flux of words; never advanced sentiment not perfectly trite, supported by Latin quotation; became Private Secretary to Lord Binkie; appointed Attache to Legation at Pumpernickel (brought home despatches of Strasburg pie); remained ten years Attache after Lord Binkie's demise; gave up diplomatic service in disgust due to slow advancement; exceedingly proud of French language skills as diplomatist
- **Return to England**: Turned country gentleman; wrote pamphlet on Malt; took strong part in Negro Emancipation; became friend of Mr. Wilberforce; had famous correspondence with Reverend Silas Hornblower on Ashantee Mission; gave speech at Quashimaboo-Aid Society; in London during Parliament, in May for religious meetings; in country as magistrate and visitor among destitute; said paying addresses to Lady Jane Sheepshanks (Lord Southdown's third daughter); criticized Rebecca's backgammon-playing as godless
- **Religious Activities at Queen's Crawley**: Subjected servants to devotional exercises; brought father Sir Pitt to join; patronized Independent meeting-house in Crawley parish; when Miss Crawley comes alone, obliged to pretermit usual devotional exercises
- **Political Ambition**: Very earnest that old gentleman should yield up his place in Parliament; Sir Pitt constantly refuses; both too prudent to give up fifteen hundred a year; family estate much embarrassed; income from borough of great use to house

**Rawdon Crawley (Younger Son)** [CHARACTER]
- **Background**: From Sir Pitt's first marriage; at Eton licked brother Pitt violently; at college and in army had debts paid by Miss Crawley once or twice
- **Character and Lifestyle**: Perfect and celebrated "blood," or dandy about town; expert in boxing, rat-hunting, fives court, and four-in-hand driving; belonged to household troops around Prince Regent; fought three bloody duels giving proofs of contempt for death; great contempt for Queen's Crawley; seldom came except when aunt Miss Crawley paid annual visit
- **Relationship with Miss Crawley**: She took fancy to him as boy, sent him to Cambridge, bought him commission in Life Guards Green when asked to quit; almost adopted him; disliked elder nephew Mr. Pitt exceedingly, despised him as milksop; never horrified at his courage, always paid debts after duels; "He will sow his wild oats," she says, "and is worth far more than that puling hypocrite"
- **Current Status**: Known to come in for bulk of Miss Crawley's seventy-thousand-pound property; very large young dandy, six feet high, speaks with great voice, swears a great deal, orders about servants who adore him; very generous of his money; keepers last week almost killed bailiff and his man come to arrest Captain; Rebecca performed country-dance with him (FACT from Mrs. Bute's account—she actually complimented his steps, unprecedented since she won't visit Lady Crawley except when sister in country)

**Miss Crawley (Unmarried Half-Sister)**
- **Background and Character**: Inherited large fortune from mother; old lady, silly and romantic; disliked Mr. Pitt exceedingly, despised him as milksop; became very attached to Rawdon as boy
- **Financial Position**: Possesses seventy thousand pounds in five per cents; has almost adopted Rawdon; signified intention of leaving inheritance between Rawdon and family at Rectory; preferred security of funds to lending on mortgage to Sir Pitt; described as "dear soul" who looks very apoplectic
- **Lifestyle and Views**: Leaves toady Miss Briggs at home when in country; has great deal of humour; her brothers adore her

**Mrs. Bute Crawley (Rector's Wife)**
- **Background**: Amiable pupil of Miss Pinkerton, sprightly and accomplished Miss Martha MacTavish in her youth
- **Character and Appearance**: Little, black-faced old woman in turban, rather crooked, with very twinkling eyes; refused to visit Rosa (Lady Crawley), saying would never give pas to tradesman's daughter; brother Sir Pitt had better of her in innumerable family transactions; bright eyes spy out everything at Hall; doings at Hall great food for conversation at Rectory
- **Recent Actions**: Reports Rebecca is artful hussy with dreadful designs; wrote to Miss Pinkerton inquiring about Rebecca; now suddenly taken great fancy to Rebecca—invited girls to Rectory saying their cousins will be happy to see them (PLAN: hopes to get Rebecca as piano professor for her children); paid Rebecca score of compliments about pupils' progress; actually complimented Rebecca and Rawdon's country-dance steps together (unprecedented honor from proud woman first cousin to Earl of Tiptoff)

**Reverend Bute Crawley (Rector, Uncle to Mr. Pitt)**
- **Appearance and Character**: Tall, stately, jolly, shovel-hatted man; far more popular in county than Baronet brother; at college pulled stroke-oar in Christchurch boat; thrashed best bruisers; carried taste for boxing and athletic exercises into private life
- **Social Activity**: Not a fight, race, coursing match, regatta, ball, election, dinner within twenty miles he didn't attend; could be seen at Fuddleston, Roxby, Wapshot Hall with great county lords; had fine voice; sang "A southerly wind and a cloudy sky"; rode to hounds in pepper-and-salt frock; one of best fishermen in county

**Other Characters and Information**
- **Miss Pinkerton**: Headmistress at Chiswick; receives letter from Mrs. Bute Crawley (former pupil) asking about Rebecca; responds noting Rebecca was pupil, appearance disagreeable, parents disreputable, but talents considerable, principles hitherto correct; dread lest mother's low principles prove hereditary; sure nothing will injure Rebecca's principles in refined circle of Sir Pitt Crawley
- **Lady Crawley (Rosa)**: Indolent, void of character; during Miss Crawley's visit and gaieties, mostly upstairs taking pills; tradesman's daughter (per Mrs. Bute Crawley)
- **Miss Rose Crawley**: Daughter, age ten; thin, insignificant
- **Miss Violet Crawley**: Daughter, age eight; thin, insignificant; rude boisterous tastes; knows where hens lay eggs; climbs trees; rides young colts; discovers jam-pot haunts; battles with Rose
- **Amelia Sedley**: Rebecca's friend; gave her India muslin and pink silk now worn; Rebecca writes to her
- **Miss Briggs**: Miss Crawley's toady, left at home when Miss Crawley in country
- **Miss Tuffin**: Governess candidate recommended by Miss Pinkerton; eighteen, daughter of late Reverend Thomas Tuffin (Fellow of Corpus College, Cambridge); exceedingly pleasing appearance; can instruct in Syriac and Constitutional law; objectionable in Sir Huddleston Fuddleston's family
- **Miss Letitia Hawky**: Governess candidate recommended by Miss Pinkerton; twenty-nine; pitted with small-pox; halt in gait, red hair, obliquity of vision; morally and religiously virtuous
- **Sir Huddleston Fuddleston**: Family where governess needed; neighbor of Rector Crawley
- **Lady Fuddleston**: Dear friend of Mrs. Bute Crawley
- **Scattered narrative mentions**: Conar, Thidrek Corrett, Islan Lindner, Dadette Lindner, Jolia Hollett (and others apparently background figures)

## Critical Facts and Status
- Parliamentary seat at Queen's Crawley worth fifteen hundred a year; family estate much embarrassed; income from borough of great use to house
- Rebecca has successfully gained upper hand of entire Queen's Crawley household—her accomplishment as governess complete within summer of second year
- Miss Crawley's seventy-thousand-pound inheritance disputed reversionary spoil between Rawdon and Rector's family
- Mrs. Bute Crawley has now taken Rebecca into her confidence and favor despite earlier reports of her being artful hussy
